module_title: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: Foundational Architecture
introduction: This foundational level explores the structural anatomy of the CPC. It distinguishes between substantive rights and procedural rules, defines the ultimate outcomes of a suit (Decree vs. Judgment), and explains the core doctrines that prevent the multiplicity of lawsuits.

core_concepts.title: Structure of the CPC
core_concepts.description:
The CPC is uniquely divided into two distinct parts:
1. The Body (158 Sections): Lays down the substantive/general principles of jurisdiction. Sections can ONLY be amended by the Parliament.
2. The Schedule (51 Orders & Rules): Lays down the actual procedure/method to implement the Sections. Orders can be amended by the High Courts to suit local needs.

core_concepts.title: Decree, Judgment, and Order (Section 2)
core_concepts.description:
Understanding the outcome of a civil suit:
- Decree (Sec 2(2)): The formal expression of an adjudication which conclusively determines the rights of the parties regarding all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit. It can be preliminary or final.
- Order (Sec 2(14)): The formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is NOT a decree. (e.g., an order granting an adjournment).
- Judgment (Sec 2(9)): The statement given by the Judge on the grounds of a decree or order. (It is the detailed reasoning behind the decision).

core_concepts.title: Res Sub Judice (Stay of Suit) - Section 10
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'A matter under judgment'.
- The Rule: No court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties, pending in a competent court.
- Purpose: To prevent courts of concurrent jurisdiction from simultaneously entertaining parallel litigations, which could lead to conflicting decisions.

core_concepts.title: Res Judicata - Section 11
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'A matter already judged'.
- The Rule: Once a competent court has finally decided an issue between two parties on the merits, neither party can file a fresh lawsuit on the exact same cause of action.
- Purpose: Based on three Latin maxims: (1) *Nemo debet bis vexari* (No man should be vexed twice for the same cause), (2) *Interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium* (It is in the interest of the State that there be an end to litigation), and (3) *Res judicata pro veritate accipitur* (A judicial decision must be accepted as correct).

important_entities.name: Jurisdiction of Courts (Sections 15-20)
important_entities.key_fact: Where must a civil suit be filed?
important_entities.significance: Section 15 mandates that every suit shall be instituted in the court of the 'lowest grade competent to try it'. For immovable property, it is filed where the property is situated (Sec 16). For movable property or compensation for wrongs, it can be filed where the wrong was done OR where the defendant resides/works (Sec 19).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'Res Judicata in Writ Petitions' Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners often ask: 'Does Res Judicata apply to Writ Petitions under Article 32 or 226?' **YES**. The Supreme Court has clarified that the general principle of Res Judicata applies to writ proceedings to prevent endless litigation. **EXCEPTION:** It does NOT apply to the writ of *Habeas Corpus*.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Judgment is the 'Why', Decree is the 'What'.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The Judgment provides the detailed reasoning (the why), while the Decree formally states the final relief/rights granted (the what).

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which doctrine prevents the trial of two parallel suits on the same issue?', select **Res Sub Judice (Section 10)**, not Res Judicata (which bars a fresh suit after a final decision).
